subject: physics_2
question_text: How are the stationary waves formed in a closed pipe? Explain the various modes of vibrations in a closed pipe and establish the relation between their frequencies.

mark_split.label: Closed pipe and its boundary condition

verification.note: The 1+2+2+2+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it — the figure carries 0 marks because the question does not ask for a diagram. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: a closed pipe holds a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so the fits are l = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 …, giving n₁ = v/4l, n₃ = 3n₁, n₅ = 5n₁ — the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 with only odd harmonics present.

recall_prompt: Say the derivation in order — the closed-pipe boundary condition, then the first, third and fifth harmonics, and the ratio.

steps.label: Closed pipe and its boundary condition
steps.mark_note: Node at closed end, antinode at open end
lines: An organ pipe with one end closed and
the other end open is a closed organ
pipe.
Sound waves reflect at the ends and
superpose, forming stationary waves in
the air column. The air at the closed
end cannot move, so a node always forms
there; the air at the open end moves
freely, so an antinode always forms at
the open end.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The two fixed facts — node at the closed end, antinode at the open end — set up every mode.
steps.why: The wall stops the air from moving (zero displacement, a node) while the open end leaves it free (maximum displacement, an antinode). Every allowed mode must satisfy both ends at once, and that is what selects the quarter-wave fits.
common_mistakes: Placing the antinode at the closed end — the wall cannot move, so the closed end is always a node.
Copying the open-pipe condition — an open PIPE has antinodes at both ends; a closed pipe has one of each.

recall.must_convey: That a closed pipe always has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
accept: the wall stops the air moving

steps.memory_tip: Wall = still air = node. Opening = free air = antinode.

steps.label: The fundamental mode
steps.margin_note: The fundamental: antinode at the open (left) end, node at the closed wall — a quarter wavelength in the pipe.
steps.why: The sketch is the boundary condition made visible: one antinode-to-node span is a quarter of a wavelength, and that single span fills the whole pipe in the fundamental.
common_mistakes: Drawing the closed wall on the antinode side — the wall belongs at the node.

recall.must_convey: That the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength: antinode at the open end to node at the closed end.
accept: draw the pipe closed at one end
antinode at the open end, node at the wall
reject: n three equals three n one

steps.memory_tip: Antinode to node is a quarter wave — the closed pipe's fundamental is exactly one such span.

steps.label: First harmonic
lines: The first harmonic (fundamental) has one
node at the closed end and one antinode
at the open end, so a quarter wavelength
fits the pipe:
With v the speed of sound in air:
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the quarter-wave fit, then n₁ = v/4l.
steps.why: One antinode-to-node span is the smallest piece of a wave that satisfies both ends, and it is a quarter of a full wavelength — that is why 4l appears under v, where the open pipe had 2l.
common_mistakes: Writing l = λ₁/2 — the half-wave fit is the OPEN pipe's; the closed pipe fits a quarter wave.
Confusing displacement with pressure — these node/antinode positions are for displacement.

recall.must_convey: That a quarter wavelength fits the closed pipe, so λ₁ = 4l and n₁ = v/4l.

steps.memory_tip: Closed pipe fundamental: quarter wave in the pipe, so 4l under the v.

steps.label: Third harmonic
lines: The next possible mode has two nodes and
two antinodes. Three quarter-wavelengths
fit the pipe:
This is the third harmonic — the first
overtone of the closed pipe.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: λ₃ = 4l/3 from the fit, then n₃ = 3n₁ — the SECOND harmonic never appears.
steps.why: Adding one node-antinode pair adds half a wavelength — two more quarters — to the quarter-wave fit, taking it from 1 quarter to 3. The count jumps 1 → 3, skipping 2: the closed pipe cannot sound the even harmonics.
common_mistakes: Calling this mode the second harmonic — the frequency is 3n₁, so it IS the third harmonic; no mode at 2n₁ exists.
Writing l = λ₃ — one full wavelength has a node at BOTH ends and cannot satisfy the open end.

recall.must_convey: That the next mode fits three quarter-wavelengths, λ₃ = 4l/3, giving n₃ = 3n₁.
accept: n three is three n one

steps.memory_tip: Each new mode adds TWO quarters, so the count goes 1, 3, 5 — odd numbers only.

steps.label: Fifth harmonic
lines: The next overtone has three nodes and
three antinodes. Five quarter-wavelengths
fit the pipe:
This is the fifth harmonic — the second
overtone of the closed pipe.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: λ₅ = 4l/5 from the fit, then n₅ = 5n₁.
steps.why: The same two-quarter jump repeats: 3 quarters become 5. Establishing this third point is what proves the pattern is 1, 3, 5 and not a coincidence of the first two modes.
common_mistakes: Numbering it the third overtone — count overtones from the fundamental: 3n₁ is the first, 5n₁ the second.
Writing λ₅ = 5l/4 — invert carefully: l = 5λ₅/4 gives λ₅ = 4l/5.

recall.must_convey: That the following mode fits five quarter-wavelengths, λ₅ = 4l/5, giving n₅ = 5n₁.
accept: n five is five n one

steps.memory_tip: Quarters count 1, 3, 5 — and the harmonic numbers copy the quarter count exactly.

steps.label: The ratio
lines: From equations (1), (2) and (3), the
fundamental and the overtones are in the
ratio:
A closed pipe produces only the odd
harmonics; the even harmonics are
absent.
steps.margin_note: Final mark. The ratio AND the sentence — only odd harmonics are present.
steps.why: The skipped even numbers are the closed pipe's signature and the standard contrast with the open pipe's 1 : 2 : 3 — the concluding sentence is the physics the whole derivation was building toward.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 : 2 : 3 — that is the OPEN pipe; the closed pipe skips every even harmonic.
Giving the ratio without the odd-harmonics sentence — the ratio is evidence, the sentence is the conclusion.

recall.must_convey: That the frequencies are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 and only odd harmonics are present.
accept: one is to three is to five
reject: one is to two is to three

steps.memory_tip: Closed pipe, closed to evens: 1, 3, 5, … only.

insider_note: One end of each kind forces quarter-wave fits, and quarter counts can only be odd — hold that one sentence and the whole 1 : 3 : 5 answer rebuilds itself.
